props.title: Licorice Pizza

sections.content: Paul Thomas Anderson's **Licorice Pizza (2021)** (2021) masterfully captures 1970s San Fernando Valley through the unlikely relationship between 15-year-old Gary Valentine and 25-year-old Alana Kane. Like Anderson's earlier **Boogie Nights** (1997), it's a love letter to Valley culture, but trades porn industry excess for entrepreneurial hustle and coming-of-age awkwardness. The film joins other recent 70s-set masterpieces like **Once Upon a Time in Hollywood** (2019) in recreating the era's freewheeling spirit while adding contemporary perspective on its social dynamics.

sections.content: Anderson's attention to period detail elevates **Licorice Pizza** beyond typical nostalgia fare. The film's waterbed business subplot echoes real 1970s entrepreneurial schemes, while the gas crisis sequence captures genuine historical tension. Like **Almost Famous** (2000), it uses music, fashion, and cultural touchstones to ground its story in a specific time and place. The film's treatment of casual racism and sexism reflects modern awareness while accurately depicting period attitudes, similar to **Mad Men** (2007-2015)'s approach to the 1960s.

The central relationship between Gary and Alana proves controversial yet compelling, walking a delicate line that recalls other age-gap romances like **Harold and Maude** (1971) and **The Graduate** (1967). Anderson handles this dynamic with surprising nuance, focusing on emotional connection over physical romance. The film's episodic structure, following various schemes and adventures, creates a rambling quality reminiscent of **Nashville** (1975) and other 70s New Hollywood classics. sections.content: **Licorice Pizza** pays homage to the New Hollywood era it depicts, particularly in its loose narrative style and authentic location shooting. The film's treatment of Hollywood figures like Jon Peters connects to other insider views of the industry like **The Last Movie Stars** (2022) and **The Kid Stays in the Picture** (2002). Anderson's direction evokes the energy of 70s filmmakers like Hal Ashby and Robert Altman while maintaining his own distinct style.
